findings.title: `unset --project` cannot clear the stale shared-file copy, but the design depends on it doing so
findings.description:
The Delete section (line 89) says `delete` "deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to." For `git.integration_branch`, that is `.context-forge.local.toml`. But two places tell the user to run `cf config unset <key> --project` to clear the stale copy in the *shared* file:
- Collision semantics (line 146).
- Walkthrough step 9 (line 259).

Under the routing as designed, that command does two wrong things:
- It deletes the developer's personal value (`legacy/value`), which is the value the collision rule exists to protect.
- It leaves the shared-file copy in place, so `cf check` keeps warning.

As a result, step 9's "confirm `cf check` is clean again" cannot pass, and the CLI has no supported way to remove a skipped stale copy. Pick one fix and state it:
- **Option (a), preferred because it adds no new surface:** for a personal key, `delete(key, 'project')` removes the key from both project files. This matches what "unset at project scope" means to a user.
- **Option (b):** in the different-value case, `migrate-personal` deletes the shared copy too. Reporting it as "discarded stale shared value X" keeps it visible.

findings.title: The checker rule and `migrate-personal` need per-file access that the "no API change" claim rules out
findings.description:
Line 49 and line 181 say `ConfigManager`'s public API is unchanged, and the only new export is `getProjectPersonalConfigPath` (line 61). Two new consumers need more than that:
- **Detection (line 142).** The checker must list the keys that are physically present in the *shared* file. `ConsistencyChecker` only reaches config through an injected, optional `ConfigManager` (`ConsistencyChecker.ts:47`), and `get()` returns only the winning value. When a key exists in both files, `get()` reports `source: 'project-personal'` and the shared copy is hidden. So the warning cannot be detected through the existing API in exactly the collision case the design describes.
- **Migration (lines 89, 144).** `migrate-personal` must read the shared file and delete a personal key *from the shared file*. Under the new routing, `delete()` can never do that. The doc calls this "the one exception … by design" but never says how it happens.

`readToml`, `resolveKey` and `deleteKey` are private module functions in `ConfigManager.ts`. Without a named API, the likely result is that the CLI or the checker re-implements TOML file access, which duplicates code and moves file I/O out of the config layer.

Name the addition. One small `ConfigManager` method is enough, for example `readProjectFile(kind: 'shared' | 'personal')` plus `deleteFromProjectFile(key, kind)`, or a single `migratePersonalKeys()` that returns per-key outcomes. Also state what the checker rule does when no `ConfigManager` is injected.

findings.title: Projects that already exist get no gitignore protection for the new personal file
findings.description:
The slice plan says `git.integration_branch` "must never be committed." The slice's Value section (line 23) promises to prevent personal settings "from being silently committed." But the gitignore line is only added by `cf init` (line 32, lines 157–159).

Every project that already exists, including this repo and every project the migration plan targets, never re-runs `cf init`. So after this slice ships:
1. `cf config set git.integration_branch … --project` creates `.context-forge.local.toml`.
2. Nothing ignores that file.
3. A routine `git add .` commits it.

That is the same leak, moved to a new file. The new checker rule (line 142) only looks for personal keys inside the shared file; it would not catch this.

The lightest fix is to call the same ensure-gitignore helper the first time `ConfigManager.set` creates the personal file, or from `migrate-personal`. Alternatively, add a `cf check` warning when the personal file exists but is not ignored.

findings.title: The read data flow can be stated as a plain precedence chain
findings.description:
Step 2's condition ("only if the key's own scope is `shared`, OR it's a personal key falling through…") is always true for any key that reaches it. So the read path is just: personal file (personal keys only) → shared file → user → default.

Writing it that way, and having `list()` reuse `get()` as it does today, removes a condition an implementer might code literally.

findings.title: Small interface consistency items
findings.description:
- **Option syntax.** The `migrate-personal` signature uses `-p, --project <id>`. The existing `config get/set/unset` commands all use `-p, --project [id]`, where a bare flag resolves the project from the current directory (`packages/cli/src/commands/config.ts:68,110,140`). Use the same `[id]` form.
- **MCP description text.** `config_get`'s description hard-codes "Resolution order: project config → user config → built-in default" (`configTools.ts:15`). Line 34 updates only the `configPaths` payload; the description string should change too so agents see the new order.

findings.title: Dependency on 914 is stricter than the plan entry but correct
findings.description: The plan entry lists "Dependencies: none." The slice declares `[914]` because it classifies `git.integration_branch` under its final name. 914 is complete, so this is accurate and blocks nothing.

findings.title: Routing inside `ConfigManager` follows the plan's two-file pattern and keeps dependencies pointing the right way
findings.description:
The plan asks to reuse "the existing user-vs-project two-file-precedence merge pattern rather than inventing a new one." The design does that:
- It reuses the same file helpers against a second path.
- Callers' `scope` parameter is unchanged.
- The shared/personal classification lives on the key definition, not at call sites.

Making `scope` a required field on `ConfigKeyDefinition` (line 115) means the compiler forces a decision for every future key. Dependencies stay within core (introspection → config), with CLI and MCP layered on top.

findings.title: Everything the plan assigns to this slice is covered, without overreach
findings.description:
The design covers each item in the plan entry:
- key classification
- file routing
- the minimal `cf init` gitignore line
- a migration/compatibility story
- the MCP config tools

The broader gitignore template stays deferred to Future Work, as the plan says. Choosing a dedicated migration command over extending the closed `fixAction` union (`types.ts:240`) is the lighter, well-justified option. Keeping `migrate-personal` minimal (line 284) is proportionate.

findings.title: Failure modes are listed for each new file write
findings.description:
The design covers:
- **Migration:** writes the personal file before deleting from the shared file, is safe to re-run, and handles each key separately, reporting `failed: <error>` per key.
- **Personal-file write:** failures surface from the existing helper.
- **`.gitignore` write:** failures abort `cf init` through `handleError`.

No new network or message paths are introduced, and the parent plan states no performance or other non-functional targets that apply.
